'''Yu Deng''' ({{Lang-zh|s=邓煜|p=Dèng Yù}}, born June 1989) is a Chinese mathematician and a professor of mathematics at the [[University of Chicago]]. He is known for his contributions to [[partial differential equations]], [[fluid dynamics]], and [[Probabilistic analysis of algorithms|probabilistic analysis]]. He was awarded the [[Fields Medal]] in 2026 for his derivation of the [[Boltzmann equation]], his derivation of wave kinetic equations from nonlinear dispersive systems, and his development of probabilistic approaches to [[non-linear dynamics]].

== Early life and education ==
Deng was born in June 1989<ref name="Cepelewicz-2026">{{Cite web|date=23 July 2026|title=Yu Deng Wins the Fields Medal 2026 for His Work on the Random Data Problem|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/yu-deng-wins-the-fields-medal-2026-for-his-work-on-the-random-data-problem-20260723/|access-date=23 July 2026|website=[[Quanta Magazine]]|language=en|last=Cepelewicz|first=Jordana|archive-date=24 July 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260724102215/https://www.quantamagazine.org/yu-deng-wins-the-fields-medal-2026-for-his-work-on-the-random-data-problem-20260723/|url-status=live}}</ref> in [[Kaifeng]], [[Henan]], China.<ref>{{Cite web |title=菲尔兹奖获得者邓煜祖籍河南开封，全家学霸！舅舅回忆和他下棋的故事|date=26 July 2026|trans-title=Fields Medalist Deng Yu’s Kaifeng Roots: A Family of Academic Prodigies as Uncle Recalls Chess Memories |url=https://www.hntv.tv/news/0/2081191287913811969 |access-date=28 July 2026 |website={{lang|zh|大象新闻|italics=no}}|author1=钟羽|language=zh}}</ref> His father was a [[software engineer]], and his mother was a [[gastroenterologist]].<ref name="Cepelewicz-2026" /> He was raised in [[Shenzhen]], Guangdong, and began participating in mathematics competitions in primary school.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Liu |first=Michael |date=21 June 2023 |title=Mathematical maestro tackles nature's greatest puzzles |url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/news/stories/math-maestro-tackles-natures-greatest-puzzles/ |access-date=19 July 2026 |website=USC Dornsife News |language=en-US |publisher=[[University of Southern California]] |archive-date=19 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260719230226/https://dornsife.usc.edu/news/stories/math-maestro-tackles-natures-greatest-puzzles/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

As a child, Deng excelled in tournaments of the Chinese strategy board game [[Go (game)|Go]].<ref name="Searcy-2026" /> In 2001, while in middle school, he competed professionally but failed to qualify for the  national Go tournament in China. He later recalled, "Either Go or math. Since I lost, I decided to move my focus to math."<ref name="Cepelewicz-2026" /> As a first-year student at [[Shenzhen Senior High School]], he won first prize at the 2006 [[Chinese Mathematical Olympiad]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=1 September 2006 |title=Deng Yu Wins Gold at the 47th International Mathematical Olympiad |url=https://news.sina.cn/sa/2006-09-01/detail-ikkntiam7724897.d.html |access-date=23 July 2026 |website=[[Shenzhen Economic Daily]] |language=zh |via=[[Sina Corporation]] |archive-date=23 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260723185157/https://news.sina.cn/sa/2006-09-01/detail-ikkntiam7724897.d.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He then represented China in the 2006 [[International Mathematical Olympiad]], where he won a gold medal at age 16.<ref name="Searcy-2026">{{Cite web |last=Searcy |first=Maureen |date=23 July 2026 |title=UChicago Prof. Yu Deng receives Fields Medal, highest honor in mathematics |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/uchicago-prof-yu-deng-receives-fields-medal-highest-honor-mathematics |access-date=23 July 2026 |website=University of Chicago News |language=en |publisher=[[University of Chicago]] |archive-date=23 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260723193409/https://news.uchicago.edu/story/uchicago-prof-yu-deng-receives-fields-medal-highest-honor-mathematics |url-status=live }}</ref>

Granted exemption from the [[Gaokao]], Deng was admitted to [[Peking University]] in 2007, the same year as [[Hong Wang]].<ref name="South China Morning Post-2026">{{Cite web |date=23 July 2026 |title=Wang Hong and Deng Yu become first Chinese nationals to win Fields Medal |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3361633/fields-medal-win-wang-hong-deng-yu-are-first-chinese-nationals-score-top-maths-honour |access-date=23 July 2026 |website=South China Morning Post |language=en |archive-date=23 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260723182605/https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3361633/fields-medal-win-wang-hong-deng-yu-are-first-chinese-nationals-score-top-maths-honour |url-status=live }}</ref> He was an undergraduate there for two years until June 2009, when he transferred to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where he graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in mathematics in 2011.<ref name="Yu Deng-2025" /> As an undergraduate at MIT, Deng developed an interest in partial differential equations and, after working on a problem given to him by [[Gigliola Staffilani]], published a paper on the [[nonlinear Schrödinger equation]] in the journal ''Analysis & Partial Differential Equations''.<ref name="Quanta2026" />

In 2015, Deng earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in mathematics from [[Princeton University]].<ref name="Yu Deng-2025" /> As a doctoral student at Princeton, Deng won a Jacobus Fellowship, the university's highest honor for graduate students.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Best |first=Zia |date=5 February 2015 |title=Four win Jacobus Fellowship, top graduate student honor |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2015/02/05/four-win-jacobus-fellowship-top-graduate-student-honor |access-date=23 July 2026 |website=Princeton News |publisher=[[Princeton University]] |language=en}}</ref> His doctoral dissertation, completed under [[Alexandru D. Ionescu]], was titled, "Long time behavior of some nonlinear dispersive equations".<ref name="Yu Deng-2025">{{Cite web |title=Yu Deng: Curriculum Vitae |url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Xd_LHE05PpgNN8eGJPzZARvZ2YE3lmLV/view?usp=embed_facebook |access-date=17 July 2026 |date=July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260719141503/https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Xd_LHE05PpgNN8eGJPzZARvZ2YE3lmLV/view?usp=embed_facebook |archive-date=19 July 2026 |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref> Ionescu recalled Deng as "brilliant from the beginning...even as a graduate student, without experience...he was very good at getting at the essence of the thing, picking up what matters in a problem."<ref name="Quanta2026" />

== Career ==
After receiving his doctorate, Deng was an instructor at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] at New York University from 2015 to 2018. He became an assistant professor of mathematics at the [[University of Southern California]] in 2018 and a full professor there in April 2024.<ref name="Yu Deng-2025"/> In September 2024, Deng joined the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]] as an associate professor of mathematics and was promoted to a full professorship in June 2025.<ref name="Yu Deng-2025" />

== Academic research ==
Deng works in [[partial differential equation]]s and [[mathematical physics]], particularly on probabilistic and combinatorial methods for nonlinear wave and particle systems. With [[Andrea Nahmod]] and Haitian Yue, he developed tools known as random tensors to study rough random initial data for the two-dimensional [[nonlinear Schrödinger equation]], proving invariance of the associated [[Gibbs measure]]. With Zaher Hani at the University of Michigan, he subsequently used combinatorial expansions of interacting waves to rigorously derive the wave kinetic equation from the Schrödinger equation over the time scales predicted by physics.<ref name="Quanta2026">{{cite magazine |last=Cepelewicz |first=Jordana |title=Amid Life's Chaos, a Meticulous Mathematician Finds Stability |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/yu-deng-wins-the-fields-medal-2026-for-his-work-on-the-random-data-problem-20260723/ |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]] |date=23 July 2026 |access-date=24 July 2026 |archive-date=24 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260724102215/https://www.quantamagazine.org/yu-deng-wins-the-fields-medal-2026-for-his-work-on-the-random-data-problem-20260723/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Deng and his collaborators adapted these methods to systems of [[hard sphere]]s. They derived<ref>{{cite arXiv| last1=Deng | first1=Yu | last2=Hani | first2=Zaher | last3=Ma | first3=Xiao | title=Long time derivation of the Boltzmann equation from hard sphere dynamics | date=2024 | eprint=2408.07818 | class=math.AP }}</ref> the [[Boltzmann equation]] from Newtonian particle dynamics over long time scales, overcoming the repeated-collision problem that had restricted earlier results to very short times. For a periodic-box model, their work combined with earlier Boltzmann-to-[[Navier–Stokes equations|Navier–Stokes]] limits to establish a rigorous passage from microscopic particle motion to macroscopic fluid behaviour in a major case of [[Hilbert's sixth problem]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Sloman |first=Leila |title=Epic Effort to Ground Physics in Math Opens Up the Secrets of Time |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/epic-effort-to-ground-physics-in-math-opens-up-the-secrets-of-time-20250611/ |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]] |date=11 June 2025 |access-date=24 July 2026 |archive-date=23 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260723183857/https://www.quantamagazine.org/epic-effort-to-ground-physics-in-math-opens-up-the-secrets-of-time-20250611/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Jo |first=GaHyeon |title=Yu Deng uses mathematics to explain gas molecules' motion and resolves a 125-year problem |url=https://www.dongascience.com/en/news/78655 |work=DongA Science |date=29 June 2026 |access-date=24 July 2026 |archive-date=24 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260724095402/https://www.dongascience.com/en/news/78655 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv | last1=Deng | first1=Yu | last2=Hani | first2=Zaher | last3=Ma | first3=Xiao | title=Hilbert's sixth problem: derivation of fluid equations via Boltzmann's kinetic theory | date=2025 | eprint=2503.01800 | class=math.AP }}</ref>

== Awards ==
In 2021, Deng received a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]] in recognition of outstanding early-career research.<ref name="South China Morning Post-2026"/> In 2025, he was awarded the [[Oberwolfach Prize]] for "his outstanding achievements in analysis and applied mathematics".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oberwolfach Prize 2025 goes to Yu Deng |url=https://www.mfo.de/about-the-institute/news/oberwolfach-prize-2025-goes-to-yu-deng |access-date=23 July 2026 |website=MFO |language=en |archive-date=20 February 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260220070246/https://www.mfo.de/about-the-institute/news/oberwolfach-prize-2025-goes-to-yu-deng |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2026, he was awarded the [[Clay Research Award]] for "remarkable derivation of the Boltzmann equation for long times, starting from a system of hard spheres".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Yu Deng |url=https://www.claymath.org/people/yu-deng/ |access-date=23 July 2026 |website=Clay Mathematics Institute |language=en-US |archive-date=24 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260724035020/https://www.claymath.org/people/yu-deng/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 23 July 2026, Deng was awarded the [[Fields Medal]] alongside [[Hong Wang]], [[John Pardon]], and [[Jacob Tsimerman]] at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in [[Philadelphia]], [[Pennsylvania]].<ref name="nytimes">{{Cite news |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=23 July 2026 |title=Four Young Mathematicians Receive Prestigious Fields Medals |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/23/science/fields-medals-pardon-deng-wang-tsimerman.html |access-date=23 July 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He and Hong Wang are the first Chinese citizens to be awarded the Fields Medal.<ref name="South China Morning Post-2026" />
